expectations.text: The core rule (invalidate cache before writing to shared state, not after) is present and stated as a general rule, not tied to a specific incident narrative
expectations.evidence: SKILL.md 'The rule' section (lines 8-19) states it generically and prominently: 'When a code path both writes shared state and invalidates a cache entry for that state, invalidate the cache first, then write the state — never the reverse. Write-then-invalidate leaves a window where a concurrent reader can repopulate the cache with data older than the write...' No entity names, ticket numbers, or company-specific detail appear in this section or in the following 'Why the order matters' / 'This is necessary, not sufficient' sections — the rule and its mechanism are phrased entirely in general cache-aside terms.

suggestions.assertion: The core rule ... is present and stated as a general rule, not tied to a specific incident narrative
suggestions.reason: This assertion is nearly guaranteed to pass regardless of skill quality — any reasonable distillation attempt will restate the given rule in some general form, since the rule itself was handed to the model in the prompt. It doesn't discriminate between a well-distilled skill and one that also leaks incident narrative elsewhere (as happened here). Consider either merging it with a narrative-freeness check or dropping it in favor of a stronger assertion (see next suggestion).

The eval's own expected_output text says the distilled skill should have 'no ticket numbers, PR references, or incident-specific narrative' but none of the four expectations actually checks for narrative content independent of the six literal reference tokens. SKILL.md's 'Case reference' section is exactly such a narrative — it retells the specific scenario ('customers who upgraded their plan intermittently kept their old limits under traffic spikes,' 'an async entitlement job') even setting the ticket numbers aside. A hypothetical output that stripped only the '#NNNN'-style tokens but kept this narrative paragraph would still pass all four current expectations, which under-tests the stated goal. Consider adding an assertion that the skill contains no case-study/incident-narrative section at all (not just no reference numbers), e.g. flagging phrases like 'this incident', 'this pattern was distilled from', or a dedicated 'case reference'/'background' section.

Expectations 3 and 4 depend on scripts/lint_skill.py, which is part of the skill's own tooling and was never available to invoke in this without_skill baseline run (no skill was loaded, and the script doesn't exist anywhere in this workspace). As written, these two expectations are structurally unverifiable — and therefore always FAIL — for any without_skill condition, which will silently drag down every baseline run's pass rate for reasons unrelated to output quality. If without_skill runs are meant to be compared against with_skill runs on the same 4-expectation rubric, consider marking lint-script-dependent expectations as N/A/skipped rather than FAIL when the tooling isn't part of the condition being graded, so aggregate comparisons aren't confounded by condition-only unavailability.

eval_feedback.overall: Expectation 1 (zero ticket/PR/issue references) is a strong, discriminating assertion and it correctly caught a real failure: the produced SKILL.md leaks all six reference tokens in a closing 'Case reference' footnote, despite the transcript explicitly reasoning that this was an acceptable provenance mention rather than 'leaning on the incident's specifics as the primary content.' That is exactly the failure mode this eval exists to detect, and it fired correctly. However, expectations 3 and 4 could not be evaluated at all in this baseline condition since scripts/lint_skill.py was never run and isn't present in this workspace — that's a structural limitation of grading a without_skill transcript against skill-tooling-dependent assertions, not a quality problem with the produced content. Net result: 1/4 pass, with the one clear failure (ticket leakage) being the most informative signal in this run.
